learn.title: Solid-State Batteries: Safer, Denser Energy Storage
learn.intro: Solid-state batteries represent a leap forward in energy storage, replacing liquid electrolytes with solid materials. They offer higher energy density and improved safety, addressing key challenges in electric mobility and grid storage. As governments push for cleaner transport, these advanced batteries could accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels.
learn.c1_text: Unlike traditional lithium-ion batteries that use flammable liquid electrolytes, solid-state batteries use a rigid or semi-solid material. This reduces fire risk significantly. Think of it like comparing a water balloon to a sponge—both hold liquid, but one bursts easily while the other stays intact under pressure.
learn.c2_text: Solid-state batteries can pack more energy into the same space because they allow for lithium metal anodes instead of graphite. This means EVs could travel farther on a single charge. Imagine fitting an entire library into a shoebox versus a regular shelf—same content, much smaller footprint.
learn.c3_text: India is investing heavily in domestic battery manufacturing through its Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. With plans to build 50 GWh of cell capacity by 2030, India aims to reduce reliance on imported batteries and support local EV adoption. The government has allocated $2.6 billion for advanced chemistry cell production.
learn.stat1: DOE estimates solid-state batteries could reach 500 Wh/kg energy density by 2030
learn.stat2: Current lithium-ion batteries average around 250–300 Wh/kg
learn.stat3: India's PLI scheme targets 50 GWh of battery cell manufacturing capacity by 2030
learn.stat4: Over 70% of global lithium-ion supply chain relies on China today

learn.title: Second Life EV Batteries for Grid Storage
learn.intro: When electric vehicle batteries retire from automotive use, they still retain up to 80% of their original capacity. Repurposing them for stationary energy storage extends their lifecycle and supports renewable integration. This circular economy approach reduces waste and lowers costs for clean energy systems worldwide.
learn.c1_text: Retired EV batteries can store solar power during the day and release it at night, acting like a home battery backup system. Imagine using your old laptop battery to run a flashlight after its main job is done—same idea, just scaled up for household or grid needs.
learn.c2_text: Reusing EV batteries cuts storage costs by nearly half compared to building new systems. IRENA reports that second-life applications can reduce capital expenditure by up to 40%. These repurposed units also delay recycling demands, easing pressure on raw material supply chains.
learn.c3_text: India plans to deploy 200 GWh of battery energy storage by 2030, with second-life batteries playing a growing role. Startups like Exicom and Tata Chemicals are piloting projects to integrate used EV packs into microgrids. Government policies encourage reuse models to meet renewable energy targets efficiently.
learn.stat1: Used EV batteries retain ~80% of original capacity when retired
learn.stat2: IRENA estimates second-life batteries lower storage costs by 40%
learn.stat3: India targets 200 GWh of battery storage deployment by 2030
learn.stat4: Global second-life battery market expected to hit $30 billion by 2030

learn.title: India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission
learn.intro: Launched in 2023, India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to position the country as a global leader in clean hydrogen production. With ambitious targets and financial incentives, the mission seeks to drive decarbonization across industries while creating jobs and export opportunities in emerging green technologies.
learn.c1_text: India plans to produce 5 MMT (million metric tonnes) of green hydrogen annually by 2030. This requires massive investments in electrolyzer manufacturing and renewable energy capacity. Think of it as planting a forest of hydrogen plants fed by solar and wind farms to power heavy industry cleanly.
learn.c2_text: Under the mission, the government offers up to ₹19,744 crore (~$2.6 billion) in subsidies for green hydrogen projects. Producers receive viability gap funding and tax breaks. It’s like giving seed money to startups—but for entire industrial ecosystems aiming to go carbon-neutral.
learn.c3_text: Green hydrogen aligns with India’s goal to achieve 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030. Heavy industries like steel, cement, and fertilizers—which are hard to electrify—are prime candidates for hydrogen use. India also eyes exporting hydrogen to neighboring countries, boosting energy security and trade.
learn.stat1: India targets 5 MMT of green hydrogen production by 2030
learn.stat2: Government allocates ₹19,744 crore (~$2.6 billion) for the mission
learn.stat3: India aims for 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity by 2030
learn.stat4: Green hydrogen can cut CO₂ emissions in steelmaking by over 90%

learn.title: Green Ammonia: Clean Fuel for Shipping
learn.intro: Green ammonia, made using renewable-powered electrolysis, is emerging as a zero-carbon fuel for sectors difficult to electrify—like long-haul shipping and aviation. It also serves as a base for carbon-free fertilizers, offering dual benefits for climate action and food security in a warming world.
learn.c1_text: Ammonia burns without emitting CO₂ and can be stored more easily than pure hydrogen. Think of it like switching from coal-powered trains to electric ones—but for ships navigating oceans. Major shipping firms like Maersk are already testing ammonia-fueled engines for future fleets.
learn.c2_text: Traditionally, ammonia synthesis uses natural gas, releasing CO₂. Green ammonia uses renewable electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen, then combines hydrogen with nitrogen. This process eliminates emissions, making fertilizers sustainable—a vital step toward climate-resilient agriculture.
learn.c3_text: India plans to become a top exporter of green ammonia, leveraging cheap solar and wind power. Projects underway include ACME’s $1.6 billion plant in Rajasthan and Reliance’s proposed hub in Gujarat. The government supports this via tariff waivers and infrastructure development under the National Green Hydrogen Mission.
learn.stat1: Green ammonia production could reduce fertilizer sector emissions by 180 million tons/year globally
learn.stat2: Shipping accounts for ~3% of global CO₂ emissions
learn.stat3: India has identified 50 sites suitable for green ammonia manufacturing
learn.stat4: IRENA projects green ammonia trade may reach $150 billion by 2050

learn.title: Sodium-Ion Batteries: Affordable Alternative
learn.intro: Sodium-ion batteries offer a promising alternative to lithium-ion, using abundant sodium instead of scarce and costly lithium. While slightly less energy-dense, they’re safer, cheaper, and environmentally friendlier. Ideal for large-scale storage and budget-friendly EVs, they could democratize access to clean energy storage.
learn.c1_text: Sodium is found in seawater and table salt, making it virtually limitless. Unlike lithium, which requires mining in ecologically sensitive areas, sodium extraction is low-impact. Think of it like choosing tap water over bottled mineral water—same hydration, far greater availability.
learn.c2_text: These batteries avoid expensive materials like cobalt and nickel, reducing costs by up to 30%. They’re also less prone to thermal runaway, meaning fewer fire risks. Like switching from sports cars to reliable sedans—they may not be fastest, but they're practical and affordable.
learn.c3_text: India is researching sodium-ion tech through partnerships with startups and IITs. Given its large-scale salt production and growing EV market, India could benefit from domestically producible storage solutions. Government initiatives promote R&D in alternative chemistries to diversify beyond lithium dependence.
learn.stat1: Sodium is 1,000x more abundant than lithium in Earth’s crust
learn.stat2: Sodium-ion batteries cost ~30% less than lithium-ion counterparts
learn.stat3: IRENA forecasts sodium-ion market to exceed $10 billion by 2030
learn.stat4: India produces over 25 million tons of salt annually

learn.title: Electric Buses and Trucks: Commercial Electrification
learn.intro: Electrifying commercial vehicles like buses and trucks is critical to cutting urban pollution and transport emissions. Unlike passenger cars, these high-mileage fleets offer significant impact per vehicle converted. Countries investing in electric public transit see cleaner air, lower noise, and reduced fuel costs for municipalities.
learn.c1_text: Electric buses eliminate tailpipe emissions and operate more quietly than diesel versions. Cities like Shenzhen have fully electrified their bus fleets—over 16,000 units—cutting CO₂ by thousands of tons yearly. Imagine replacing roaring engines with silent glides through city streets.
learn.c2_text: Medium- and heavy-duty trucks pose bigger hurdles due to range and charging time constraints. However, advances in battery tech and overnight depot charging make electrification feasible for delivery routes. Think of upgrading from steam locomotives to modern electric trains—efficiency improves dramatically over time.
learn.c3_text: India aims to electrify 50% of new bus purchases and 30% of new car sales by 2030. The Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme has supported over 1.4 million EV registrations so far. State transport corporations are procuring thousands of electric buses under the initiative.
learn.stat1: India targets 50% of new bus purchases to be electric by 2030
learn.stat2: Shenzhen became first city to fully electrify its 16,000+ bus fleet
learn.stat3: Over 1.4 million EVs registered under India’s FAME scheme
learn.stat4: Medium-duty electric trucks can save operators $20,000+ annually in fuel costs
